content.title: What is Garbage Collection?
content.description: Garbage Collection (GC) is Java's automatic memory management mechanism that identifies and removes objects that are no longer reachable, freeing heap memory for future use.

content.content: Unlike languages that require developers to manually allocate and free memory, Java automatically manages memory using the Garbage Collector. It periodically scans the heap, identifies objects that are no longer referenced by the program, and reclaims their memory, helping prevent memory leaks and improving application stability.

content.title: Why Garbage Collection?
content.content: Garbage Collection automates memory management, reduces programmer effort, minimizes memory leaks, and helps improve application reliability.

Java stores objects in the heap memory. When an object is no longer referenced by any part of the application, it becomes eligible for garbage collection. The JVM automatically removes such objects during a garbage collection cycle.

content.title: Key Idea
content.description: An object is eligible for garbage collection only when it is no longer reachable by any live reference.

content.content: Objects become eligible for garbage collection when their references are removed or become inaccessible.

content.title: Nullifying a Reference
content.code:
Student s = new Student();
s = null; // Object becomes eligible for GC

content.title: Reassigning a Reference
content.code:
Student s1 = new Student();
s1 = new Student(); // First object becomes eligible for GC

content.content: The JVM automatically decides when to perform garbage collection. Developers can request it using System.gc(), but the JVM is not obligated to execute it immediately.

content.title: Important
content.content: Calling System.gc() is only a request. The JVM decides whether and when garbage collection actually occurs.
The Java heap is generally divided into generations to optimize garbage collection performance.

rows: Very low pause times for large heaps

content.title: Garbage Collection
content.time_complexity: Depends on heap size, algorithm, and number of live objects
content.space_complexity: Requires additional JVM memory for GC metadata and processing

items.question: Web Applications
items.answer: Automatically manages memory for large numbers of user requests.

items.question: Enterprise Systems
items.answer: Maintains application stability during long-running execution.

items.question: Android Applications
items.answer: Helps reclaim memory for mobile applications.

items.question: Cloud Services
items.answer: Optimizes memory usage in distributed applications.

content.title: Cleaning an Office
content.content: Imagine an office where employees discard old papers they no longer need. A cleaning staff periodically removes those unused papers, creating space for new work. Garbage Collection performs the same task by removing unused objects from memory.

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Garbage Collection, heap memory, eligible objects, System.gc(), generations, G1 GC, Parallel GC, Serial GC, ZGC, memory leaks, and JVM memory management are among the most frequently asked Java interview topics.

items.question: Does System.gc() guarantee immediate garbage collection?
items.answer: No. It only requests the JVM to perform garbage collection.

items.question: Can developers manually destroy Java objects?
items.answer: No. Memory is automatically reclaimed by the JVM.

items.question: Is an object garbage collected immediately after becoming unreachable?
items.answer: Not necessarily. The JVM determines the appropriate time for collection.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: Garbage Collection automatically frees memory occupied by unreachable objects, allowing developers to focus on application logic rather than manual memory management.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Garbage Collection automatically manages heap memory.
Only unreachable objects are eligible for GC.
System.gc() is only a request to the JVM.
Heap memory includes Young Generation, Old Generation, and Metaspace.
Modern JVMs provide collectors such as G1 GC and ZGC.
Automatic memory management reduces memory leaks and simplifies development.
